newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks to put Mideast peace efforts on track.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks to put Mideast peace efforts on track.

text.p: President Bill Clinton hoped to use talks on Monday with Israel's prime minister to revive Mideast peace efforts, but will not embrace his call for a direct U.S. role in talks with the Palestinians.
Clinton and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were slated to hold Oval Office talks on some new ideas that U.S. officials hope will defuse tensions over new Jewish settlements in Arab East Jerusalem.

Vice President Al Gore, however, made clear on Sunday night that Clinton was not receptive to Netanyahu's public suggestion that it may take U.S.-led negotiations, like those conducted by President Jimmy Carter in 1978 at Camp David, to break the current impasse.
"Issues must be resolved through direct give-and-take negotations between the parties involved. That is the only true path to success," Gore said in outlining the administration's guiding principles.
"The United States cannot and will not seek to impose its will upon either side," Gore told some 2,500 delegates attending a policy conference of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

"Outside pressures will only be counterproductive and will only serve to undermine the peace process," Gore said. "Only the parties can determine the future of their people. ... We do not believe that Jerusalem or other permanent status issues are appropriate for others to decide."

Netanyahu has proposed that he and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat reach a final peace agreement within six months -- and said the goal may require an intensive three-way summit like the one that led to accords between Egypt and Israel.

During the Camp David negotiations, Carter most often met separately with Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin and Egyptian President Anwar Sadat -- pressuring each one to move closer to the position of the other.
The current crisis erupted over Israel's decision to build Jewish settlements in Arab East Jerusalem, a move that has angered most Palestinians.
The United States continues its policy of opposing all new Israeli settlements in the disputed territory, but has thus far muted its public criticism in hopes of finding a way to defuse tensions.

Violence has erupted nearly every day since Israel broke ground last month on Har Homa, a 6,500-home project on a hilltop that Palestinians call Jabal Abu Ghneim. Both sides claim the land as their own.
Before coming to Washington, Netanyahu on Sunday flew to Minnesota to meet with Jordan's King Hussein, who was in a hospital following prostate surgery.

White House officials privately have been cool to the idea of trying to solve all of the thorny issues separating the Israelis and Palestinians at one time, believing that a slow but steady process would be more realistic.

Palestinians view Netanyahu's offer of go-for-broke talks as a ploy to circumvent interim accords that already require him to hand over occupied land. They see Har Homa as a unilateral act that violates an agreement to negotiate the Jewish settlement issue.

It was unclear whether Netanyahu would offer Clinton a gesture to revive U.S.-backed peacemaking launched in 1993. A final deal would have to tackle the toughest issues -- Jerusalem, borders, Jewish settlers and Palestinian refugees.

White House and State Department officials have been searching for ways to defuse the situation by coming up with compromises acceptable to both sides. "We are developing our own ideas and we're going to put them forward," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
